title: Week 109 · Lesson 133: Pediatric Respiratory Illness — FNP-Level Bronchiolitis, Croup, Asthma and Pneumonia Safety
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 109 — Lesson 133: Pediatric Respiratory Illness

FNP-level goal: Assess respiratory physiology before diagnostic labels, distinguish common upper- and lower-airway syndromes by age and pattern, avoid low-value bronchiolitis treatment, initiate evidence-based care within scope, and recognize children who need oxygen, emergency stabilization, or higher-level evaluation.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize increased work of breathing, hypoxemia, fatigue, apnea, and impending respiratory failure.
  • Differentiate bronchiolitis, croup, asthma, pneumonia, pertussis, and foreign-body aspiration.
  • Apply evidence-based bronchiolitis care without routine imaging, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, or antibiotics.
  • Use age, history, examination, oxygenation, and response to treatment to select diagnostics and disposition.
  • Provide a clear home-care and escalation plan for stable children.

Part 1 — Physiology Before Etiology

Children can compensate for respiratory disease and then deteriorate rapidly. Begin with airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and hydration. Observe from the doorway: position, interaction, speech or cry, color, respiratory rate, retractions, nasal flaring, head bobbing in infants, grunting, stridor, wheeze, and symmetry.

Severe retractions, cyanosis, apnea, silent or minimal air movement, altered consciousness, exhaustion, poor perfusion, or inability to speak, cry, drink, or feed safely requires emergency support. A falling respiratory rate in a tiring child can be more dangerous than persistent tachypnea.

Part 2 — Age Narrows the Differential

In infants, consider bronchiolitis, pertussis, pneumonia, congenital heart disease, airway anomaly, aspiration, and sepsis. In toddlers, add croup and foreign-body aspiration. In school-age children and adolescents, asthma, pneumonia, dysfunctional breathing, and other causes become more prominent. Age does not exclude disease, but it changes probability and expected presentation.

Ask onset, progression, fever, cough quality, stridor, wheeze, apnea, cyanosis, feeding, urine, choking, prior episodes, atopy, prematurity, cardiopulmonary disease, immune status, exposures, vaccines, smoke or vaping, travel, and treatment response.

Part 3 — Bronchiolitis Pattern

Bronchiolitis typically begins with viral upper-respiratory symptoms in a young child and progresses to cough, tachypnea, increased effort, wheeze or crackles, and feeding difficulty. Diagnosis is clinical. The AAP recommends against routine radiography or laboratory testing in a typical presentation because nonspecific findings can prompt unnecessary antibiotics.

Risk of severe disease increases with young age, especially under 12 weeks, prematurity, underlying cardiopulmonary disease, immune compromise, apnea, dehydration, or worsening work of breathing. Repeated assessment matters because feeding and fatigue can change during the illness.

Part 4 — Bronchiolitis Treatment Is Supportive

Supportive care includes nasal suction when secretions impair feeding, hydration support, monitoring oxygenation and work of breathing, and oxygen when persistent hypoxemia meets the applicable pathway. The AAP guideline advises against routine albuterol, epinephrine, systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics, and chest physiotherapy for bronchiolitis.

This does not mean doing nothing. It means directing treatment at physiology rather than prescribing therapies that do not improve the typical disease course. Antibiotics are appropriate only when a bacterial infection is identified or strongly suspected.

Part 5 — Croup Is an Upper-Airway Problem

Croup commonly causes a barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor after viral symptoms. Severity depends on stridor at rest, retractions, air entry, color, fatigue, and mental status—not merely the loudness of cough. Keep the child calm because agitation worsens obstruction.

Corticosteroid treatment is commonly used across severity levels, while nebulized epinephrine is used for more significant obstruction with observation for recurrence according to local protocol. Stridor at rest with marked retractions, cyanosis, drooling, tripod positioning, toxic appearance, or poor air movement requires urgent or emergency evaluation and consideration of alternate diagnoses such as bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis.

Part 6 — Asthma Pattern

Asthma involves variable airflow obstruction and airway inflammation. Recurrent episodes, triggers, nighttime or exercise symptoms, atopy, family history, and improvement with bronchodilator support the diagnosis. Wheeze is not required, and not every wheezing infant has asthma. Severe asthma may produce a quiet chest because airflow is critically reduced.

Assess symptom frequency, exacerbations, steroid or emergency use, hospitalization, adherence, inhaler and spacer technique, environmental exposure, and comorbid rhinitis, obesity, reflux, or sleep disorder. Acute management and long-term controller decisions should follow current age-specific asthma guidance and an individualized action plan.

Part 7 — Pneumonia

Pneumonia becomes more likely with fever, tachypnea, focal crackles or reduced breath sounds, hypoxemia, pleuritic pain, or focal respiratory findings. Viral and bacterial presentations overlap. Chest radiography is not automatically required in every stable outpatient case but is useful when diagnosis is uncertain, hypoxemia or significant distress is present, complication is suspected, or treatment failure changes management.

Antibiotic selection depends on age, immunization, severity, allergy, local resistance, and likely pathogen. Reassess when fever or respiratory symptoms worsen, hydration declines, or improvement does not occur as expected.

Part 8 — Foreign-Body Aspiration

Sudden cough, choking, unilateral wheeze or reduced breath sounds, unexplained persistent symptoms, or abrupt onset while eating or playing should raise concern. A normal chest radiograph does not reliably exclude an aspirated foreign body. Do not perform blind finger sweeps.

Complete obstruction requires emergency choking response appropriate to age. A stable child with suspected retained airway foreign body still needs urgent specialist or emergency evaluation because migration and delayed inflammation can occur.

Part 9 — Pertussis and Apnea

Pertussis may begin with mild catarrhal symptoms and progress to paroxysmal cough, inspiratory whoop, posttussive emesis, or apnea. Young infants may have apnea or cyanosis without a classic whoop and can become critically ill. Ask about immunization and household cough, obtain testing according to timing and public-health guidance, and address treatment, isolation, and exposed contacts.

Any apnea, cyanosis, poor feeding, or respiratory exhaustion in a young infant requires urgent evaluation.

Part 10 — Oxygenation and Testing

Pulse oximetry must be interpreted with waveform quality, perfusion, motion, baseline disease, altitude, and clinical appearance. A normal oxygen saturation does not eliminate significant work of breathing, and a spurious low value should be verified without delaying care for a distressed child.

Viral testing may support infection-control or treatment decisions in selected cases but does not replace physiology. Order imaging and laboratory tests when they will change diagnosis, disposition, or treatment—not as automatic respiratory panels.

Part 11 — Hydration Is Part of Respiratory Care

Tachypnea, fever, nasal obstruction, and fatigue reduce intake and increase fluid loss. Ask about feeds, vomiting, urine, and ability to coordinate suck-swallow-breathe. Small frequent fluids or oral rehydration may help a stable child; significant work of breathing can make oral intake unsafe and requires higher-level support.

A respiratory diagnosis is not safely managed at home if the child cannot maintain hydration.

Part 12 — Prevention and Longitudinal Care

Review influenza, COVID-19, pertussis, pneumococcal, and other age-appropriate immunization; smoke and vaping exposure; hand hygiene; asthma trigger reduction; spacer technique; and respiratory-virus prevention strategies for eligible high-risk infants under current guidance. Address housing and medication access because inability to obtain an inhaler or safe sleep space changes risk.

Part 13 — Disposition

Outpatient care requires comfortable oxygenation, mild and nonprogressive work of breathing, adequate hydration, alert mental status, reliable caregivers, and clear follow-up. Same-day reevaluation is warranted for worsening cough or fever, new focal findings, reduced intake, uncertain diagnosis, or poor response.

Emergency care is required for cyanosis, apnea, severe retractions, grunting, stridor at rest with distress, drooling or tripod position, silent chest, altered consciousness, exhaustion, poor perfusion, persistent significant hypoxemia, suspected complete obstruction, or inability to hydrate safely.

Clinical Case 1 — Typical Bronchiolitis

A seven-month-old has three days of rhinorrhea followed by cough, diffuse wheeze and crackles, mild retractions, and reduced but adequate intake. Oxygenation is acceptable and the infant is alert. The FNP uses clinical diagnosis, nasal and hydration support, and close return precautions rather than ordering routine radiography or prescribing albuterol, steroids, and antibiotics.

Clinical Case 2 — Stridor at Rest

A two-year-old has barking cough, stridor at rest, suprasternal retractions, and agitation. The FNP minimizes distress and arranges urgent treatment and observation under a croup pathway; worsening air entry, cyanosis, drooling, or fatigue would require emergency airway support.

Clinical Case 3 — The Missing Choking History

A three-year-old suddenly coughed while eating nuts and now has persistent unilateral wheeze. The FNP treats foreign-body aspiration as urgent even if an initial radiograph is normal, rather than labeling this new-onset asthma.

FNP High-Yield Framework: BREATHE

  1. B — Begin with severity: airway, effort, oxygenation, fatigue, perfusion, mental status.
  2. R — Relate age and onset: infant versus child, gradual viral course versus sudden choking.
  3. E — Examine the pattern: stridor, wheeze, focal crackles, asymmetry, silent chest.
  4. A — Assess intake and risk: hydration, apnea, prematurity, cardiopulmonary or immune disease.
  5. T — Treat the syndrome: supportive bronchiolitis care, croup or asthma pathway, targeted antibiotics only when indicated.
  6. H — Hold low-value testing: image or test only when results can change care.
  7. E — Escalate and educate: emergency signs, technique, follow-up, prevention.

Take-Home Summary

Pediatric respiratory safety starts with work of breathing and fatigue, not with the diagnostic label. Bronchiolitis is usually a clinical diagnosis with supportive treatment; stridor localizes upper-airway risk; recurrent variable symptoms support asthma; and sudden asymmetry demands a foreign-body differential.

Educational note: Follow current AAP bronchiolitis guidance, age-specific asthma and croup protocols, public-health recommendations, and local emergency pathways. Apnea, cyanosis, severe retractions, stridor with distress, silent chest, altered consciousness, exhaustion, poor perfusion, significant hypoxemia, or unsafe oral intake requires urgent care.
